title: Word Flip
statement: Write a function `reverseWords(s)` that takes a string and returns a new string with the order of the words reversed. Words are separated by one or more spaces. Leading, trailing, and extra internal spaces must be removed, and words in the result must be separated by exactly one space. An empty input (or one with no words) returns an empty string.
constraints: s contains only letters, digits, and spaces
followUpPrompts: Can you solve it without using split()?
What happens with multiple consecutive spaces?
interviewerProbes: What happens if the string is empty or contains only spaces?
How are you handling multiple spaces between words?
What is the time complexity of your approach?
Why did you choose this data structure or method?

title: Most Frequent Element
statement: Write a function `mostFrequent(arr)` that returns the element that appears the most times in an array of integers. If several elements tie for the highest frequency, return the one that reaches that frequency first while scanning from left to right. The array always contains at least one element.
followUpPrompts: Can you do it in a single pass?
How would you change the tie-breaking rule to return the smallest element instead?
interviewerProbes: Why did you choose a hash map here?
How do you handle ties between elements?
What is the complexity of this approach?
What happens if the array has only one element?

title: Digital Root
statement: Write a function `digitSumUntilSingle(n)` that repeatedly sums the digits of a non-negative integer until the result is a single digit, and returns that digit. For example, 9875 → 9+8+7+5 = 29 → 2+9 = 11 → 1+1 = 2, so it returns 2.
followUpPrompts: Can you solve it in O(1) time without any loops?
Why does the repeated-digit-sum relate to modulo 9?
interviewerProbes: What happens when n is 0?
Is there a constant-time formula for this?
What approach are you considering?
What is the complexity of this approach?

title: Count Pairs With Sum
statement: Write a function `pairWithSum(arr, target)` that returns the number of index pairs (i, j) with i < j such that arr[i] + arr[j] === target. Count each qualifying index pair once — duplicate values produce separate pairs.
followUpPrompts: How would your solution change if the array were already sorted?
Why is a nested loop not good enough here?
interviewerProbes: Can you solve this in one pass with a hash map?
How do you count duplicate values correctly?
What happens if the array is empty?
What is the complexity of this approach?
Why did you choose this data structure?

title: Longest Distinct Substring
statement: Write a function `longestUniqueSubstring(s)` that returns the length of the longest contiguous substring of `s` in which no character repeats. For example, in "pwwkew" the answer is 3 ("wke" — note that "pwke" is a subsequence, not a substring).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
expectedSpaceComplexity: O(K) where K is the alphabet size
followUpPrompts: Why does the two-pointer window avoid re-scanning characters?
How would you return the substring itself instead of its length?
interviewerProbes: What are the left and right pointers responsible for?
When exactly do you shrink the window?
Can you avoid the extra space here?
What is the complexity of this approach?

title: Bracket Balance
statement: Write a function `balancedBrackets(s)` that returns true if a string consisting only of the characters ( ) [ ] { } is properly balanced. Every opening bracket must be closed by the same type of bracket and in the correct nested order. An empty string is considered balanced.
followUpPrompts: Why does this problem naturally fit a stack?
What is the earliest point at which you can return false?
interviewerProbes: Why did you choose a stack for this?
What happens if the string is empty?
What happens if a closing bracket appears when the stack is empty?
What is the complexity of this approach?

title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
statement: Write a function `mergeIntervals(intervals)` that takes an array of intervals [start, end] and returns a new array with all overlapping or touching intervals merged. Two intervals touch when one's end equals the other's start, e.g. [1,4] and [4,5] merge into [1,5]. The result must be sorted by start.
followUpPrompts: Why is sorting by start the key first step?
What breaks if you compare only start values when merging?
interviewerProbes: What approach are you considering first?
How do you decide two intervals overlap?
What is the complexity of this approach?
Can you avoid the extra space here?

title: Product Except Self
statement: Write a function `productExceptSelf(arr)` that returns an array `out` where out[i] is the product of every element of `arr` except arr[i]. You must not use division anywhere in your solution. Aim for O(N) time.
constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer
expectedSpaceComplexity: O(1) extra beyond the output array
followUpPrompts: Why is division disallowed — what breaks with zeros?
How do prefix and suffix products combine here?
interviewerProbes: Why can't you just divide the total product by arr[i]?
What happens when the array contains zeros?
Can you do it without two extra arrays?
What is the complexity of this approach?

title: Best Single Trade
statement: Write a function `maxProfitOneTrade(prices)` where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may complete at most one trade: buy on one day and sell on a strictly later day. Return the maximum profit achievable; return 0 if no profitable trade exists.
followUpPrompts: Why does tracking the minimum price so far work?
How would this change for at most two trades?
interviewerProbes: What happens if the array is empty or has one price?
What state do you carry as you scan left to right?
What is the complexity of this approach?
Why did you choose this approach over brute force?

title: Water Collected
statement: Write a function `waterCollected(heights)` where each element is the height of a vertical bar of width 1. After it rains, water settles in the valleys between bars. Return the total units of water that remain trapped. Bars at the very edges can never hold water.
followUpPrompts: Explain why the smaller side determines the water level.
Can you do this with two pointers instead of prefix arrays?
interviewerProbes: What determines how much water sits above one bar?
Why do you move the pointer on the smaller side?
Can you avoid the extra space here?
What is the complexity of this approach?
What happens with fewer than 3 bars?

title: Longest Palindrome Slice
statement: Write a function `longestPalindromicSubstring(s)` that returns the longest contiguous substring of `s` that reads the same forwards and backwards. If several substrings tie for the longest length, return the one that starts earliest in the string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
expectedTimeComplexity: O(N^2) expected; O(N) with Manacher's as a stretch
expectedSpaceComplexity: O(1) extra for the center-expansion approach
followUpPrompts: Why must you check both odd and even length centers?
How would Manacher's algorithm improve this?
interviewerProbes: What approach are you considering?
Why do you need to expand around two kinds of centers?
What is the complexity of this approach?
How do you break ties between equal-length palindromes?

title: Island Count
statement: Write a function `countIslands(grid)` where grid is a 2D array of 1s (land) and 0s (water). An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically, surrounded by water. Return the number of islands in the grid. You may modify the grid in place.
expectedSpaceComplexity: O(R * C) worst-case for the traversal stack
followUpPrompts: Why does recursion depth matter on a 200x200 grid?
How would you solve it without mutating the input?
interviewerProbes: Are you using DFS or BFS, and why?
How do you avoid visiting a cell twice?
What happens if the grid is entirely water?
What is the complexity of this approach?
Why did you choose this data structure?
